1:
Gill, Henry and Wesley take the two visitors for two of the three who had stood with Abraham at Hebron in the heat of that same day, the created angels sent to execute God's purpose on Sodom; Ellicott notes that the verse simply continues the preceding chapter. Calvin puts the question the others pass over: why has one of the three suddenly disappeared? He dismisses the Jewish answer that one came to destroy and the other to preserve, since Moses shows both assisting in the rescue. His own account is that Abraham received a peculiar favour, God sending not merely two messengers from the angelic host but manifesting himself familiarly in his own Son, one of the three holding the principal place; and since Christ made himself known more obscurely to Lot than to Abraham, only the two came down to Sodom.

Lot sitting in the gate tells Ellicott a good deal, none of it flattering. Lot had become a citizen, probably after the deliverance from the Elamite invasion, when as Abraham's kinsman he would have been honoured; that respect, Ellicott thinks, made him close his eyes to the sinfulness of the people, live inside the town, and let its citizens marry his daughters, while intercourse with Abraham had apparently ceased and he had lost his share in the covenant of circumcision. Henry reads the same posture warmly. There was but one good man in Sodom and the messengers soon found him out, which he turns into a rule, that wherever we are we should enquire out those who live in the fear of God, as countrymen seek each other abroad. Lot distinguished himself from his neighbours that night, and Henry marks the consequence sharply: he that did not act like the rest must not fare like the rest. He sat in the gate at evening while the rest, it is likely, were tippling, waiting for a chance to do good, and bowed to the ground before men whose bearing was sober though they came in no state, as if he discerned something divine in them at first view. Calvin will not go so far. Many contend Lot sat there daily to receive guests, but since Moses gives no cause it would be rash to affirm it; he grants Lot was not sitting idle, yet thinks it no less likely he had come out to meet his shepherds and see the sheep folded.

Gill has Lot address them as persons of quality, with majesty in their countenances, not knowing them for angels, entertaining them unawares as the apostle says. Their refusal is read as deliberate. Clarke notes that some manuscripts turn the negative into a word meaning to him, giving and they said unto him, we lodge in the street, the negation understood; knowing the temper of the inhabitants and passing for mere travellers, they preferred the open air, until Lot's vehemence and their knowledge that he was righteous overcame them, though they were not yet willing to make themselves known. He compares our Lord on the road to Emmaus, who made as though he would go further and then yielded to his disciples' importunity. Ellicott explains the street as the broad open space of the town and observes that in a warm climate, before caravanserais existed, sleeping out was no hardship for travellers who found no host. Calvin makes the refusal a test. The angels withhold assent so as to investigate the holy man's disposition, and by pretending it is safe to sleep on the highway they conceal what they know of the city; for if gates are shut against wild beasts and enemies, it is absurd that those within should face worse dangers than those without. They speak so, he says, to make the wickedness of the people appear the greater, and Lot's pressing shows all the more plainly how careful he was of his guests.
4:
Henry says the night's work filled the measure, and proved the cry of Sodom no louder than there was cause for. What strikes him first is that the wickedness was universal: old and young, from every quarter, unanimous in a vile design, the old not past it and the young already come up to it, so that either the city had no magistrates or they were themselves aiding and abetting. Wesley repeats him almost word for word. Ellicott gets the same from the Hebrew, which reads from the end and may mean either to the last man or from the very end of the town; either way there were not ten righteous men in Sodom to save it. Calvin calls the single crime a lively picture of the place. Their consent in wickedness was diabolical, since they conspired so readily; their lust blind and impetuous, since they rushed together without shame like brute animals; their cruelty plain in their besieging a house in a collected troop. He infers they were not contaminated with one vice only but given up to every audacity in crime, and cites Ezekiel on the beginnings from which they had come to this, and Paul on God punishing impiety by a blindness in which men dishonour their own bodies.

Calvin reads the demand itself as a piece of pretence. Their intention was to abuse the strangers, but their words claim another object: as though Lot, himself a sojourner, had offended by admitting unknown men into the city, they imperiously require the guests to be produced. The Greek translators took the verb in a carnal sense, and Calvin grants that Scripture modestly uses the word so, but thinks these men would have spoken coarser language had they meant it, and that the sentence covers the design. Clarke will not describe the crime, saying only that this account justifies the character given of the people in the preceding chapter, that the offence is too bad to describe and sufficiently marked in the text, and that it is punished with death in his own country. When Lot goes out and shuts the door behind him, Calvin finds a rare virtue: he preferred the safety of guests he had undertaken to protect above his own life, and such magnanimity is required of God's children where duty is concerned. Gill explains the address brethren: not by family, since the Sodomites came of Ham and Lot of Shem, nor by religion, the one being idolaters and the other a worshipper of the true God, but by community of nature and long neighbourhood, the soft language used only to win them off their purpose.

The offer of his daughters nobody defends outright. Clarke says nothing but the sacred light in which eastern nations held the rights of hospitality could palliate it, a host being bound to defend his guest at the cost of his own life; and even so he calls the words not only anxious solicitude but unwarrantable haste. Calvin treats it as a defect mixed with great virtue: destitute of advice, Lot devised an unlawful remedy, and though pressed by necessity and dealing with wild beasts, he should rather have endured a thousand deaths than ward off one evil by another. From it Calvin draws a prayer, that when God gives the spirit of invincible fortitude he would also govern us by the spirit of prudence. Wesley states the rule flatly: of two evils we must choose the less, but of two sins neither, nor ever do evil that good may come. Ellicott presses hardest of all. He grants Ambrose's plea that a smaller sin was substituted for a greater, and Chrysostom's that hospitality bound Lot to protect his guests, but answers that fatherhood bound him equally to protect his daughters, and that if men might substitute smaller sins for greater they would have an excuse for every wickedness.
9:
The answer Lot gets shows, in Calvin's phrase, the indomitable haughtiness of this people. They threaten that if he persists they will deal worse with him than with those he defends, then reproach him that a foreigner should assume a judge's province. Every word proves their pride: they set one man against a multitude, as if to ask by what right he alone claimed authority; they boast that they are natives and he a stranger; they plead their long succession and find it intolerable to be reproved. Ellicott sharpens both halves from the Hebrew. The one came to sojourn is said as though a great concession had been made in letting Lot live inside their walls, citizenship being jealously guarded then and the sojourner's position bitter; while he will needs be a judge stands in the Hebrew as is ever acting as a judge, implying that Lot had reproved them before, as Peter says of his righteous soul vexed from day to day. Clarke infers that his sitting in the gate may after all mark a magistrate's place.

Calvin notices that Moses still calls the rescuers men, though they were not, and though they now begin to exert their celestial force they do not yet declare themselves angels sent from heaven. What he takes from it is a rule about timing. The Lord may for a while seem regardless while the faithful are in conflict, but never deserts his own and stretches out his hand at the critical moment; in preserving Lot he defers aid until the last extremity. We are therefore to wait on his providence with tranquil minds and follow our calling undaunted, since though he suffer us to be exposed to danger he will show he was never unmindful of us. Calvin also sees an exchange in the door. Lot had shut it to protect his guests, and is repaid when the angels not merely receive him back through it but set the barriers of divine power against the men outside; what they bring is not human help but assistance armed from heaven.

What the blindness was, the three commentators answer differently. Gill takes it for a peculiar stroke, blindness of eye and heart together on Aben Ezra's reading, and observes that the Hebrew word occurs only twice; it cannot be blindness as to every object, since men wholly blind would not have wearied themselves about Lot's house but would have been glad to grope their way home. He adds that had they not been given up to judicial blindness and hardness of heart, such a stroke might have convinced them their ways were evil, whereas they pressed on the harder. Clarke sets out two readings and prefers neither: either the angels deprived them of the regular use of sight, or brought on a darkness so deep the door could not be found, plainly the view of the writer who says they were compassed about with horrible great darkness. Ellicott argues it out. Actual blindness is not meant in either place where the word occurs, since blinded men would have fled in terror or groped until they found the door, and an army of blind men could not have been led from Dothan to Samaria. In both cases, he says, the men did not know anything had happened to them: the Sodomites thought they saw the door, the Syrians thought they knew the country. He defines the word as a disturbance of vision in which the eye is not in proper connection with the brain, so the men of Sodom seemed always just about to reach the door, and pressed and strove and quarrelled, and always failed, as they supposed through one another's fault. Wesley asks only what it was for, and answers that it was meant to put an end to the attempt and to be an earnest of their utter ruin the next day.
12:
Gill marks the change: once they had drawn Lot back inside, the visitors began to make themselves known and to tell him their errand. Calvin thinks the timing deliberate, their last act having been so gross that Lot must see it was impossible for God to bear with them longer. The reason they give, that the cry of the city was waxen great, he reads as a statement about accumulation rather than a single offence: God was provoked not by one act but, after long forbearance, almost compelled by an immense mass of crimes to come down and punish. The more sins men heap together, Calvin says, the higher their wickedness rises and the nearer it comes to God to cry for vengeance; so the words that testify to his long-suffering also declare what awaits those who, having gathered mountains of guilt, exalt themselves with daily increasing audacity, as if like the giants they meant to assail heaven. He adds a second reason for the explanation: not only that Lot might ascribe praise to God's righteousness, but that being struck with fear he might hasten his going.

Henry and Wesley both stop at the fact that angels bring the sentence. The holy angels are ministers of God's wrath for the destruction of sinners as well as of his mercy for the preservation of his people, and in that sense, Henry says, the good angels become evil angels. Calvin defends the same point at length against an objection. Scripture does ascribe the kinder office to them, calling them ministering spirits sent forth for those who shall inherit salvation; it also says God executes his judgments by evil angels. Calvin's answer is that God sets his elect angels over the judgments he carries out by means of the reprobate; it would be absurd to give devils the honour of presiding over God's judgments, since they yield no voluntary obedience but are only reluctantly compelled to serve as his executioners. It is no office foreign to the elect angels to come down armed to punish, as one destroyed Sennacherib's army in a night.

The question put to Lot, whether he has any besides in the city, Henry reads as both a command and a favour. The command is that he do all he could for those about him, snatching them as brands out of the fire, since those delivered by grace out of a sinful state ought to work for the deliverance of others, above all their own relations. The favour is in the terms: they do not ask whether Lot knows any righteous men in Sodom fit to be spared, for they knew there were none, but only what kindred he has there, so that righteous or unrighteous they might be saved with him. Bad people, Henry observes, often fare better in this world for their good relations' sake. Clarke works out who these were from the grammar. The word is singular here and plural in the next verse, and since Lot appears to have had two daughters there were two; nor were they yet married, only betrothed, as the earlier verse shows in calling them women who had not known man. Reckoned part of Lot's household, they were entitled on that account to the offer of protection, and Clarke is clear that they did not take it: they treated the warning as a ridiculous tale, the creature of Lot's invention, and doubtless perished notwithstanding the grace sincerely offered them. Ellicott reads the participle as the takers of his daughters, which is why Ewald and Tuch render it of men still only to marry them; he keeps the traditional sense, confirmed by the next verse, where the two daughters are those found with him, implying Lot had others besides. On the reception Lot met he notes that the Hebrew is as one laughing, that is, not in earnest.
15:
Lot had the whole night to prepare, Ellicott notes, and spent part of it on the errand to his sons-in-law; yet when morning came he was not ready. Why he lingered is answered four ways. Gill canvasses three guesses, that he was loath to leave his goods, or waiting for his sons-in-law, or praying the city might be spared, but prefers a fourth: he was so filled with horror at the coming judgments that he stood stupefied, with no power to stir, which he thinks best agrees with the Hebrew. Ellicott says flatly that Lot clung to his wealth and could not make up his mind to leave it. Clarke supposes him still pressing useless entreaties on the family who would not come. Calvin, having praised Lot's faith, says Moses shows something human still adhered to him. He guesses at the fear behind it: Lot saw himself going into exile, and doubted what would become of a fugitive who had left house and furniture behind and must go naked and in want into some desert place. What he failed to consider is that he must act like men in a shipwreck, who cast their cargo into the sea to come safe into port. He did not doubt God spoke truth, nor refuse to move, but sinking under his own infirmity he crept where he should have run; in him, Calvin says, the Spirit shows us our own tardiness as in a mirror.

The hand laid on him is read by everyone as mercy, not rescue merely. Clarke says the angels pulled them away by main force, the Lord being merciful, or they had perished in their lingering as the others perished in their gainsaying. Ellicott renders the clause in Jehovah's pity for him. Calvin finds the tardiness wonderful, since Lot was persuaded the angels did not threaten in vain and yet could be moved by no words until dragged out by their hands. Christ said the spirit is willing but the flesh weak; here, Calvin thinks, a worse fault appears, the flesh so repressing the spirit's alacrity by its sluggishness that it can scarcely creep along. The faithful should therefore prepare the more earnestly to follow God, and beware of hearing his threats as with deaf ears; and even then, he adds, they will never press forward so studiously as not to be retarded more than enough. Wesley draws the comfort out. Lot did not make a jest of the warning as his sons-in-law had, but he did not make the haste the case required, and it might have cost his life had the angels not taken his hand; if God had not been merciful to us, our lingering had been our ruin. Keil and Delitzsch note that the plural gives way to a singular when the charge is spoken, and that referring it to one of the two angels sits awkwardly, since Lot answers him by the name of God.

Clarke takes the charge word by word and finds every one emphatic. Escape for thy life: the danger is imminent, life and soul both at stake. Look not behind thee: there is barely time, and a single look back may prove fatal. Neither stay in all the plain, since God will destroy that as well as the city. Escape to the mountain, on which these judgments shall not light and which God has appointed him for a refuge. This is no ordinary judgment, but a fire from heaven that will burn up the cities, the plain, and all who remain in either. He observes that the charge begins and ends by addressing Lot's own feelings, on the principle that all a man has he will give for his life, self-preservation being nature's first law. Ellicott adds that the word rendered consumed means swept away, and Keil that the mountain meant is the range afterwards called the mountains of Moab.
18:
Gill notices a small oddity: Lot speaks as though three were present, not having observed that the two who brought him out had gone, though he addresses only one, the one who had bidden him make for the mountain. Calvin turns the same detail into a point of doctrine. That Lot, seeing two, directs his speech to one shows he was not relying on the angels at all; he was well convinced they had no authority of their own and that his salvation was not in their hands, and he used their presence only as a mirror in which the face of God might be contemplated. Calvin approves, too, of the way Lot begins by rehearsing the mercy already shown him. He does it not so much to testify gratitude as to gain confidence in asking more, and that is right, since the goodness of God is neither exhausted nor wearied by giving, so the readier we find him the bolder we may hope; it is the property of faith to take encouragement for the future from past favour.

The request itself Calvin will not excuse. Lot does not simply obey, nor let himself be preserved in God's way, but contrives a new method of his own: God assigns him a mountain and he chooses a city instead. Those who extol his faith here, treating the words as a model of prayer, are mistaken; Moses means rather to show that Lot's faith was not entirely pure or free from defect. Calvin lays down the axiom that our prayers are faulty so far as they are not founded on the word, and observes that Lot does not merely depart from the word but indulges himself preposterously against it, and such importunity has no affinity with faith. The sequel, he adds, is the punishment of that foolish cupidity: a sudden change of mind, since all who will not submit to God necessarily vacillate, and no sooner attain one wish than a fresh disquietude arises and forces them to change their minds again.

The reasons Lot gives are handled more gently by the others. Clarke explains I cannot escape to the mountain as a miscalculation made under pressure: Lot saw the destruction so near that he thought there was not time enough to reach it, forgetting that God gives his creatures no command impossible to fulfil, though the hurry and perturbation of his mind, Clarke says, will at once account for and excuse so gross an oversight. Ellicott renders the following clause literally, lest the evil overtake me, meaning the threatened calamity itself rather than any mishap on the road. On the plea that the town was a little one Clarke offers two motives: either Lot wanted it for an inheritance and urged its smallness so that the request might be the more readily granted, or he supposed that being little it was less depraved than Sodom and Gomorrah and so not yet ripe for punishment, which Clarke thinks was probably the case. Gill identifies the place as Bela, afterwards Zoar, and weighs the distances, which are given as two miles from Sodom, though the Jews say four and some five, reckoning that a man may walk five miles between break of day and full sunrise. On the answer Lot receives, Gill explains the Hebrew behind I have accepted thee as I have lifted up thy face, an allusion to the eastern custom by which a man coming before his superior prostrated himself to the ground and was then bidden to raise his face and stand, that being the token that his suit was granted. Wesley draws the moral from the reason given for the delay, that the very presence of good men in a place helps to keep off judgments, and marvels at the care God takes for the preservation of his people.
23:
Gill makes the sunrise do double duty. It fixes the hour of Lot's entering Zoar and of Sodom's burning, which began together, and shows what a fine morning it was, with so little appearance of the coming tempest that those already up feared nothing and those still in bed were surprised in them. It was a morning of light and joy to Lot and a dreadful one to the cities of the plain, and Gill takes the clear sky as evidence that what followed did not proceed from natural causes. Ellicott reckons the interval: Lot started at dawn, so had an hour for his flight. Henry marks the arithmetic of the rescue: though there were not ten righteous men in Sodom for whose sake it might be spared, the one righteous man among them delivered his own soul, and the married daughters perished with their unbelieving husbands while those who stayed were preserved.

The doubled name in the verse, that the Lord rained from the Lord, is the chapter's sharpest point of division. Wesley takes it for God the Son raining from God the Father, since the Father has committed all judgment to the Son, and adds that he who is the Saviour will be the destroyer of those who reject the salvation. Clarke reports that many of the primitive fathers and several modern divines read it so, and concedes that two persons named Jehovah in one verse is a strange and curious circumstance, made more remarkable in that the Jehovah who talked with Abraham and sent the two angels does not appear again until this sentence. Yet he will not build on it: the doctrine is established elsewhere, it is not plainly indicated here, and it is better not to use proofs which themselves require proof. Ellicott is blunter, tracing the Trinitarian reading to the Council of Sirmium and preferring Calvin's more correct account, that the repetition emphasises whose act it was. Calvin explains what the emphasis is for. God did not cause it to rain in the ordinary course of nature but, as with a stretched-out hand, openly fulminated in a manner to which he was not accustomed, to make plain that this rain of fire and brimstone came from no natural cause; nor was it his will that the cities be simply swallowed by an earthquake, but that the example should be the more conspicuous.

Calvin remarks on the manner of the telling. Moses relates the destruction succinctly, though the atrocity might well have demanded a copious narrative in tragic terms; he simply recites the judgment, which no words would be vehement enough to describe, and leaves it to the reader's meditation. Ellicott grants that natural agencies were used and insists this does not diminish the event: a catastrophe of nature became miraculous by the circumstances surrounding it, and we lose the benefit of Scripture's teaching if we suppose the events recorded there differed in kind from those that happen now, since with most it is simply the curtain that is drawn back. Gill supposes an earthquake accompanied the fiery tempest, notes that Strabo attributes the lake to earthquakes and eruptions of hot bituminous waters without mentioning fire from heaven, and observes that the bitumen pits of that country would have made such a shower burn the fiercer, until the land itself became the lake the Greeks named from bitumen. Clarke gives its dimensions and clears away the legends: that a stone will not sink in it, that no wind can ruffle it, that birds flying over drop dead, that fruit near it turns to ashes when opened. These he pronounces exaggerations or fictions, the work of superstitious monks or of travellers who knew readers delight in the marvellous. The truth, he says, is that the water is exceedingly salt, far beyond the sea's usual saltness, which is why bodies float in it that would sink elsewhere.
26:
Why she looked back is guessed rather than known. Gill notes that she walked behind Lot, his back toward her, which was itself a temptation, and offers the Targums' guesses that she wished to see the end of her father's house, or whether married daughters followed. Henry breaks the act into five faults. She disobeyed an express command, sinning after the similitude of Adam's transgression; unbelief lay at the bottom, since she questioned whether Sodom would be destroyed and thought herself still safe there; she looked back on her neighbours with more concern than was fit, their day of grace being over; she hankered after her goods, the fault Christ fastens on in saying she too much regarded her stuff; and the look showed an inclination to go back, which is why our Saviour makes it a warning against apostasy. Henry adds that as the wicked are warned by Sodom to turn from wickedness, the righteous are warned by Lot's wife not to turn from righteousness. Wesley keeps the last two.

What became of her divides them completely. Clarke sets out three opinions and endorses none: that she was changed by miracle into a mass of rock salt keeping the human figure; that tarrying too long in the plain she was struck by lightning and enveloped in the bituminous matter of that country, which, never afterwards exposed to fire, resisted air and wet and so was made permanent; or that she was consumed in the burning of the plain, the record of the judgment being itself the imperishable memorial. He remarks that Scripture says little here and commentators have made the account long by their glosses. Keil and Delitzsch hold she was not turned into anything, but killed by the sulphureous vapour and afterwards encrusted with salt, so that she resembled a statue; objects near the Dead Sea, they note, are still quickly crusted over, so what Christ refers to may be understood without supposing a miracle. Ellicott prefers a third mechanism, that the earthquake heaped up a mass of the rock salt lying in strata about the sea and she was caught in the convulsion, leaving the salt hill as her memorial, salt cones being common in that neighbourhood. Calvin does not explain the manner but defends the fact against those who ridicule it as no likelier than Ovid's metamorphoses. If God made men out of nothing, he asks, why may he not reduce them to nothing, and if that be granted, why not turn them into stones? The philosophers who deride it see miracles as great daily in nature, in the hardening of crystal, in the living animal generated from lifeless seed, in birds produced from eggs.

Abraham going back at daybreak to where he had stood Henry reads as the sequel to prayer. He went to the very spot as to a watch-tower, to see what became of his petitions; when we have prayed, Henry says, we must look after our prayers, directing prayer as a letter and then looking for an answer, or as an arrow and then looking whether it reached the mark. He distinguishes the two backward looks: Abraham beheld the smoke not as Lot's wife did, tacitly reflecting on the divine severity, but humbly adoring and acquiescing in it. Clarke imagines his astonishment at finding God could not discover ten righteous persons in four cities. Ellicott explains why the early start was needed, the place lying some miles off, and thinks the forces that overthrew the cities had been some hours at work before he reached the ravine from which the scene was visible. Calvin denies that Abraham came because he doubted; persuaded already that the angel had not spoken in vain, he sought confirmation by sight, useful to himself and to posterity, and Calvin thinks he passed the night in anguish about Lot and may have gone forward partly to meet him.
30:
Lot's leaving the town he begged for is treated as the sequel to having begged for it. Henry offers three reasons why he durst not stay: he was conscious that Zoar was a refuge of his own choosing, in which he had prescribed to God, and so could not trust his safety there; or he found it as wicked as Sodom and thought it could not long survive; or he watched the waters that began after the conflagration to overflow the plain and by degrees made the Dead Sea, and judged Zoar, on the same flat, must perish in them though it had escaped the fire. From this Henry draws his rule, that shelters of our own choosing, in which we do not follow God, commonly prove uneasy to us. Clarke says it more sharply. Foolish man ever prefers his own wisdom to his Maker's; it was wrong at first not to go to the mountain, and wrong next to leave the town after God had promised it should be spared for his sake, both arguing a strange want of faith in the truth and providence of God. He adds what governs the rest of the chapter: had Lot stayed at Zoar, the shameful transaction afterwards recorded would probably never have happened. Calvin takes the episode as proof that what men contrive by rash counsels of carnal reason never prospers. Temerity often seems successful at first, but the Lord at length curses whatever is undertaken without his approval, and Isaiah's woe is fulfilled against those who begin a work and not by the Spirit of the Lord. Commanded to the mountain, Lot chose Zoar; granted Zoar, he repents and trembles at a destruction hastening on a place so near Sodom.

The cave is felt by all as a fall. Keil and Delitzsch place it in the Moabitish mountains, among caves in which the limestone rocks abound. Ellicott sets the contrast plainly: the patriarch whose wealth was once so great that he and Abraham could not dwell together is now content with a miserable home in one of them, having taken courage at the sight of the smoking valley and remembered the command he had first refused. Henry finds it strange that Lot did not return to Abraham, who had twice been the means of his safety, and answers that some good men are not wise enough to know what is best for themselves; Lot was now glad, he notes, to go to the very mountain God had appointed for his shelter. Wesley turns it into a warning: this is what men bring themselves to who forsake the communion of saints for secular advantage.

What the daughters supposed is set out carefully, since it bears on how their act is judged. Keil and Delitzsch say they were impelled by the desire to preserve their family, and mark the limits of their ignorance: they did not imagine the whole race had perished in the vale of Siddim, but feared no man would link himself with them. Clarke reasons further. Our father is old means he was not likely to marry again; there is not a man in the earth means none left, as they supposed, in all Canaan of their own kindred. As for the men of Zoar, the daughters knew that town had been devoted to destruction with Sodom and Gomorrah and was spared only at their father's asking; having lived among them they probably found them ripe for punishment, and would have thought a marriage there dangerous and criminal. Gill attends to which daughter speaks. The firstborn is the elder of these two, though daughters married in Sodom were probably older still; Aben Ezra suggests Lot had an earlier wife who died and that these were by a second. The proposal comes from the elder, Gill thinks, as being the bolder, with more authority and a greater power to persuade.
32:
Gill supposes the wine was part of the provision carried out of Zoar. On the plan itself the commentators divide over how much can be said for it. Clarke argues the most favourable construction the case will bear, on four grounds: that the daughters do not appear to have acted from any base or sensual desire; that they may have thought marriage into another family criminal, their intended husbands, probably of their own kindred, having perished at Sodom; that they may have supposed no other way was left of preserving the family; and that they expected their father to refuse as profane what they judged necessary. Ellicott concedes less. The wish to preserve seed was a very strong feeling in ancient times, and affords, he says, the sole excuse for the revolting conduct of these women; the degradation of Lot and his family is the most painful part of the story, which ends in his intense shame.

How far Lot himself is chargeable is the sharper question. Clarke thinks him in many respects excusable, since he had no accurate knowledge of what happened on either night and cannot be supposed to have been drawn away by his own lust; he might well have judged some servant brought from Zoar had been in his bed. Clarke thinks him deceived in the wine too, either not knowing its strength after a life spent among flocks, or given wine of more than usual power, an old man unused to it being easily overcome. Gill refuses that plea. Lot must have known the strength of wine as well as his daughters, and they plainly knew it, since they used it upon him; and though he may have drunk the more freely to drown his grief for his wife and goods and the children lost in Sodom, this will not excuse drinking to excess. Calvin holds the middle ground and states it as a rule: because his drunkenness was the cause of his sin, Lot's guilt is diminished but not annulled. He finds it strange the man's senses were so overcome, and suspects God struck him with a spirit of stupor beyond what wine alone would do; and if God did not spare the holy patriarch, Calvin asks, how shall we go unpunished for the same excess? He is severe on those who make Lot the protector of their own wickedness, and would have us look rather at the horrible scandal into which immoderate wine brought him.

That the same thing happened a second night strikes Gill as the aggravation of the whole business, since Lot ought to have been on his guard, knowing how he had fallen the night before. Calvin makes it a lesson about the first step. Whoever is once caught in Satan's snares involves himself deeper and deeper, so we must resist the first beginnings, since those once stupefied by the sweetness of a vice can hardly avoid losing themselves in it; every flattering temptation is to be feared as poison. What he finds most worth attention is the reversal of circumstances. Among the Sodomites, where crimes were heaped up until they nearly defiled heaven and earth, Lot lived chaste as an angel, and Calvin thinks it was the knowledge of the evil surrounding him that kept him watchful and afraid; no sooner is he safe on the mountain than Satan besieges him with new pitfalls. On the names Gill reports the derivations offered for Moab, from a phrase meaning of the father, so that the elder daughter was so far from shame that she left the fact in her son's name for all time, though others compound the word differently. Keil and Delitzsch note only what the text says, that the one became father of the Moabites and the other of the children of Ammon, and remained so to the day the words were written.
